newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban, opposition gear up for fresh fighting.
newsitem.headline: Taleban, opposition gear up for fresh fighting.

text.p: Afghanistan's Islamic Taleban militia and its foes are gearing up for fresh battles for control of Kabul and other parts of the country, spokesmen for both sides said on Monday.
There has been little change on front lines north of the Taleban-held capital for the past week or so, though the opposing forces batter each other in daily artillery battles.
"We are getting prepared, but before we attack Kabul we should take other steps," said Dr Abdullah (one name), spokesman for former government military commander Ahmad Shah Masood.
"We will take Kabul, but it will be weeks rather than days or months," he told Reuters by satellite telephone.

"There should be more activities in the eastern provinces. We have already started in Laghman (province), where we have captured some ground. We expect things to happen in Kunar (province) and Jalalabad very soon," he said.

The Taleban captured the eastern city of Jalalabad, astride Kabul's main supply route from Pakistan, a few days before they seized the capital from the former government of President Burhanuddin Rabbani in September.
The militia, which controls at least two-thirds of Afghanistan, wants to extend its strict Islamic rule throughout the country, ravaged by war for the past 18 years.

Abdullah said the other parties in the tripartite opposition alliance -- Jumbish-e-Milli led by ethnic Uzbek General Abdul Malik, and the mainly Shi'ite Moslem Hezb-i-Wahdat -- were also preparing to attack the Taleban.

He said opposition forces were preparing for action in the northwestern province of Badghis, where Malik's troops face the Taleban, and in Maidan Shahr, a mountainous region west of Kabul where Hezb-i-Wahdat confronts the purist Islamic militia.
"In Badghis, we have moved from a defensive to an offensive position, and in Maidan Shahr our allies are also getting ready," said Abdullah, speaking from northern Afghanistan.
However, a Taleban spokesman in the southern city of Kandahar said the Taleban were preparing for an unspecified operation north of Kabul, but did not say when it would start.
"We are ready to defend Kabul," Mullah Syed Mohammad Haqqani told the Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press news service. "We will defeat any opposition attack."
He said the Taleban had not lost any ground in Badghis and accused neighbouring Iran of funnelling military supplies, including landmines, to opposition forces.

Haqqani said the Taleban were ready to cooperate with peace efforts led by the United Nations, but said there could be no talks with the opposition until Taleban prisoners in the northern city of Mazar-i-Sharif were released.

The Taleban briefly occupied Mazar-i-Sharif in May when Malik cooperated with them to oust former Uzbek warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum. But Malik swiftly turned against his new-found allies and many Taleban fighters were killed. Many more, including several Taleban leaders, were taken prisoner.
Abdullah recalled that many analysts had written off the opposition before the Taleban lost Mazar-i-Sharif.
"Many people assessed us as being finished. They said we would be destroyed, but when we take action, I think that you will find that the wait was justified," he said.

Abdullah denied that the opposition offensive had lost impetus. Four weeks ago, Masood's men swept forward from the foothills of the Hindu Kush range, 80 km (50 miles) north of Kabul, to a new front line just 20 km (12 miles) from the city.
"We are not in a hurry, but that does not mean that we will wait forever before we take Kabul," he said.

The United Nations stepped up its search for peace in Afghanistan with the arrival in the region this month of former Algerian Foreign Minister Lakhdar Brahimi, newly appointed as a special envoy of U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan.
But there are few signs that the Taleban and their foes are now ready to settle their conflict at the negotiating table.
